tip.title: Quiz yourself instead of rereading
tip.why: In a 2006 experiment, students studied a prose passage and then either reread it or took a recall test on it. A week later the students who had been tested remembered far more than those who reread, even though rereading felt more effective in the moment. Pulling an idea out of memory is itself what makes it stick.
how: After reading something you want to keep, close it and write down everything you remember in two minutes.
Open it again and fix the gaps in a different color.
Repeat tomorrow and again in a few days, for just the gaps.
tip.ask: What could I write down from memory right now about the last thing I read?

markets.headline: Chips led a narrow election-day rebound and Apple weighed on the Dow; the S&P 500 added 0.36% and Tesla slipped before the results came in.
points: The S&P 500 closed at 7,568.92 (+0.36%), ending a three-day losing streak, while the Nasdaq rose 0.83% to 25,372.01 and the Dow fell 0.38% to 51,786.72. Most S&P 500 stocks still fell, and the Nasdaq-100 stayed about 10% below its record, in correction territory.

Chipmakers drove the gains after a multi-day selloff: Nvidia rose 2.29% to $206.69 and Broadcom 3.07% to $332.13, with AMD, Micron and Intel also higher. Intel gained about 4% to $62.34 after losing roughly 45% in October.

Apple dragged the Dow after warning that memory chip costs could squeeze its margin, and Palantir also fell. Brent crude slipped about 1% to near $103 on hopes of an Iran deal, and Treasuries weakened on solid job-openings data.

Tesla fell 1.32% to $398.50 before Democrats' midterm gains became clear; its shares and SpaceX's were down roughly 4% in Wednesday premarket trading. AMD reported record third-quarter results after the bell, with a fourth-quarter outlook above estimates.

pick.name: Broadcom
pick.what: Broadcom designs networking chips, custom AI accelerators and infrastructure software, and sells to the large cloud companies building AI data centers.
pick.why: It sits on the networking and custom-silicon side of the AI buildout, the part of the trade that bounced hardest when chip stocks rebounded on Nov. 3. StockAnalysis lists 51 analysts at Strong Buy with an average 12-month target of about $527, and the $332.13 close is roughly 33% below its 52-week high of $495. An idea to research, not a recommendation.
pick.risk: The stock is still far below its high and moves with the same AI-spending worries that hit chips in October. Targets and ratings come from aggregator pages that can lag, and only two recent closes were confirmed for this edition.

btc.summary: In his Nov. 2 video on a Q4 stock market correction, Cowen says a fourth-quarter dump has now hit stocks in four midterm years in a row and that this year looks on track for the same. A summary of the video says he expects the S&P 500 to test its 200-day moving average and find a bottom within the next couple of months before rebounding, with the index already below its 50-day average. He says bitcoin looks to be dumping into a fourth-quarter low, and notes that past midterm years put their lows in the first quarter, the summer or the fourth quarter. He posted another video on Nov. 3 about the midterms and markets, but I couldn't confirm what it says.

brief.lede: Chips rebounded on election day and AMD guided above estimates, while Democrats' midterm gains hit Tesla and SpaceX shares. Anthropic's updated IPO filing shows growth slowing, and a Chinese research firm warns of a humanoid shakeout.

articles.title: Chips rebound on election day, then AMD guides above Wall Street
body: Chipmakers bounced on Tuesday after a multi-day selloff, lifting the Nasdaq Composite 0.8% to 25,372.01. The S&P 500 gained about 0.4% to **7,568.92**, ending a three-day losing streak, while the Dow slipped about 0.4% to 51,786.72 as Apple weighed on it after warning that memory chip costs could squeeze its profit margin.

Nvidia closed up 2.29% at $206.69 and Broadcom rose 3.07% to $332.13, with Micron and Intel also higher; Intel gained about 4% after losing roughly 45% in October. Brent crude slipped about 1% to near $103 a barrel on hopes of an Iran deal. The Nasdaq-100 added 0.7% but still sits about 10% below its record, which keeps it in correction territory, and analysts described the rally as narrow.

After the close, AMD reported record third-quarter revenue of about **$13.4 billion**, up 45% from a year earlier, with data center sales of $8.5 billion, up 97%. Adjusted earnings of $2.09 a share beat expectations of roughly $1.95, and published summaries put its fourth-quarter revenue outlook near $17 billion, above the $16.3 billion analysts had pencilled in. Reports differ on the premarket reaction, but one had the shares up 7.3%.

Politics may matter as much as earnings for the AI trade this week. Democrats won a decisive midterm victory, including the Texas governor's race, where nominee Gina Hinojosa has called for an immediate moratorium on new data centers and an end to tax incentives for them. Wells Fargo estimates Texas holds about **27% of U.S. data center power capacity**, and its strategist called a Democratic win there a "left-tail event" for the AI trade, CNBC reported.

What it means: AMD's numbers answer the worry that AI spending is outrunning demand, at least on the chip side. The Texas result adds a different kind of risk, about where data centers can be built and at what cost. Oracle and CoreWeave were lower Wednesday morning while other AI stocks were mixed, so the market has not settled on a verdict.

articles.title: Anthropic's updated IPO filing shows growth slowing as costs jump
body: Anthropic's amended S-1, filed Nov. 2, added its first full third-quarter numbers. Revenue for the quarter ended Sept. 30 was about **$17 billion**, up from $11.56 billion in the second quarter, and nine-month revenue reached $33.24 billion.

Growth is cooling, though. Quarter-over-quarter growth was about 47%, against roughly 144% a quarter earlier, and CNBC reported that Anthropic attributed part of the slowdown to about $600 million of price reductions. Operating expenses rose to $17.5 billion, including about $5 billion of higher-cost short-term compute and a $2 billion noncash charge tied to employee donation matching.

Summaries of the filing show that turned a $974 million second-quarter operating profit into a **$567 million operating loss**. Compute and infrastructure costs took 58% of revenue, up from 48%. The filing also lists **$895.4 billion** in purchase and lease commitments, a figure analysts are now weighing against the revenue line.

The terms are still blank: no price range or share count has been filed. Reports differ on timing, with one saying a roadshow could start the week of Nov. 9 and trading begin before Thanksgiving, and another pointing to a listing around Nov. 16. Fortune reported that institutional investors are pushing for a price at the low end of the $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion valuation range being discussed.

What it means: the story has shifted from hypergrowth to scale with heavy fixed costs. The next amended filing, with a price range, will show how much of that cost investors will accept. Disclosure: this edition is assembled with Claude, which Anthropic makes.

articles.title: A Chinese research firm expects a humanoid shakeout within three years
body: GGII, a Chinese research firm, projects that at least **15% of China's 150-plus humanoid makers** will go bankrupt or be absorbed in mergers within three years, according to a Seoul Economic Daily report on the firm's Shenzhen conference. Its general manager, Zheng Liyao, expects the first major restructuring next year.

The same forecast has China's finished-humanoid shipments topping 50,000 units this year, against about 18,000 last year. That figure covers China only. Other trackers count differently: one firm puts global shipments near 60,000 this year, and IDC counted nearly 25,000 shipped worldwide in the first half.

The squeeze shows up in prices and funding. GGII says robot joint-module prices fell about **30%** from a year earlier, with more cuts expected next year, and ITjuzi data cited in the coverage show embodied-AI funding deals fell 45% last month, from 60 to 33. One investor quoted by Jiemian said fewer than ten companies have real repeat revenue from outside customers and expects room for perhaps 20 to 30 survivors. Morgan Stanley has also warned of a shakeout, citing IPOs running ahead of demand.

What it means: volume is real, since companies like AgiBot reported thousands of units shipped in the first half, but cheap parts and a funding pullback are squeezing the weakest makers. I found only the one report on GGII's forecast, so treat the exact percentages as one firm's view.

articles.title: Tesla slips on the Texas result as Cybercab heads to Shanghai
body: Tesla and SpaceX shares fell in premarket trading on Wednesday after Democrats won the Texas governor's race and made broad gains in the midterms. Reuters put the declines at about 3.6% for Tesla and 3.8% for SpaceX; other trackers showed larger drops, and an earlier after-hours move was closer to 1.8%. Tesla had closed Tuesday at **$398.50**, down 1.32%.

Investors cited several worries: tighter oversight of Tesla's driverless operations, scrutiny of government contracts held by Musk's companies, and possible inquiries tied to his political spending. Reuters reported that Musk spent nearly half a billion dollars backing Republican candidates, and Hinojosa has opposed a possible sale of a beachfront state park to SpaceX.

On the product side, Tesla's Cybercab makes its China debut at the China International Import Expo in Shanghai, which runs **Nov. 5 to 10**. Reports describe a gold finish, butterfly doors and no steering wheel, with an Optimus robot displayed alongside. The European display tour starts at Auto Zürich the same day.

What it means: Tesla's stock now trades on two stories at once. The product story is a show-floor tour that puts the Cybercab in front of new audiences, while the political one is about how much regulatory friction a Democratic Texas adds for its robotaxi plans. The premarket moves are not closing prices, so Wednesday's close will be the first real read.

articles.title: Bitcoin sits near its 200-day average as ETF money keeps leaving
body: Bitcoin traded between about **$76,000 and $77,000** on Tuesday, down roughly 12% for 2026 as of Monday's close and hovering near its 200-day moving average, which one analyst put around $76,460. U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs lost about $398.6 million on Nov. 2 and another $115.6 million on Nov. 3, according to Farside data cited by crypto.news, so the outflow slowed but did not stop.

Binance published a zero-knowledge proof of reserves for 10 major tokens from its Oct. 31 snapshot after the roughly $6.3 billion hack, a method that lets users check their balances are backed one-to-one. A broader snapshot was planned for Wednesday and takes 40 to 50 hours to prove, so full results should land later in the week. Binance says it has replaced about 95% of the affected assets.

Its SAFU insurance fund now holds about 7,500 BTC after a 7,499 BTC draw, roughly half what it held, and Binance has promised to rebuild it toward $1 billion without giving a date. The FBI has attributed the attack to North Korea's TraderTraitor group.

Analyst Benjamin Cowen is tying bitcoin to stocks. In a Nov. 2 video he argued that fourth-quarter corrections have hit equities in each of the last four midterm years, and a summary of it says he expects the S&P 500 to test its 200-day average before bottoming within a couple of months. Cowen has changed his calls before, so read it as one view.

What it means: with ETF flows negative and a stock correction possible, bitcoin's main support is the 200-day average. The Binance reserve proof due this week is the near-term trust test for the exchange.

articles.title: Starship Flight 15 gets an FAA planning date, but no license yet
body: The FAA's latest planning slide, posted Oct. 29, lists Starship Flight 15 for **Nov. 12**, moved from Nov. 8 on an earlier slide. Observers stress that it is an agency planning date, not a SpaceX announcement, and that no launch license for the flight has been issued.

Booster 22 and Ship 42 have both completed static fires. The flight aims to catch both stages with the launch tower, and recovering the upper stage needs its own license. Dates usually firm up about a week out, when SpaceX posts a mission page and the FAA issues airspace closures, so the real signal should come around Nov. 5.

SpaceX now trades publicly, and its shares fell alongside Tesla's on the Texas result, so a flight date lands on a stock already reacting to politics. Elsewhere, Google's Suncatcher prototype, four TPU chips on a satellite launched aboard a Falcon 9, has run its first workload, and Google plans two more satellites in 2027.

Coverage notes it can run only one chip at a time for about 20 minutes, and Google's energy head said space data centers can cost up to **100 times** more than ground ones. SpaceX has said it expects to start deploying orbital AI compute satellites as early as 2028.

What it means: Nov. 12 is a target to watch, not a plan to count on, since slips are common. Orbital computing is still at the test stage, so expect announcements well ahead of anything that changes where AI runs.

vocab.def: A soft whispering or rustling sound.

cards.b: From Latin susurrus, 'a whisper', a word that imitates its own sound
murmur, rustle, whisper
leaves, quiet voices, or water, anything that sounds like soft whispering

examples: A susurrus of leaves followed him down the trail.
The susurrus of the crowd settled as the lights went down.
vocab.ex: A susurrus of leaves followed him down the trail.

vocab.def: The earthy smell of rain falling on dry ground.

cards.b: Coined in 1964 by two Australian scientists from Greek petra, 'stone', and ichor, the fluid in the veins of the gods
the smell of rain, wet-earth scent
the fresh smell that rises when rain hits dry soil or pavement

examples: The petrichor after the first storm made the whole street smell alive.
She opened the window just to breathe in the petrichor.
vocab.ex: The petrichor after the first storm made the whole street smell alive.

vocab.def: Cheerful, quick readiness to do something.

cards.b: From Latin alacer, 'brisk, lively'
eagerness, readiness, promptness

vocab.ex: She accepted the invitation with alacrity.

vocab.def: Sweet and smooth to hear, like a voice or piece of music that flows easily.

cards.b: From Latin mel, 'honey', and fluere, 'to flow': literally 'flowing with honey'
dulcet, silken, honeyed
voices, music or prose that sounds smooth and pleasing

examples: The radio host's mellifluous voice made even the traffic report soothing.
She read the poem in a mellifluous whisper that quieted the room.
vocab.ex: The radio host's mellifluous voice made even the traffic report soothing.

vocab.def: Calm, peaceful and happy, often describing a time in the past that now seems golden.

cards.b: From Greek halkyon, a mythical kingfisher said to calm the winter seas while it nested
tranquil, idyllic, golden
a stretch of time you remember as untroubled, as in 'halcyon days'

examples: They talked about the halcyon summers they spent by the lake.
The long, quiet Sunday felt halcyon after a loud week.
vocab.ex: They talked about the halcyon summers they spent by the lake.

vocab.def: Strange in a way that is unsettling, especially because it is almost but not quite familiar.

cards.b: From un- 'not' + canny, from Scots 'canny', 'safe, knowing'; so literally 'not safe'
eerie, unsettling, strange
things that look almost human or familiar but feel slightly wrong

examples: The robot's smile was so close to real that it felt uncanny.
There was an uncanny quiet on the street after midnight.
vocab.ex: The robot's smile was so close to real that it felt uncanny.

vocab.def: Cheerful and full of energy and enthusiasm.

cards.b: Latin ebullire, 'to bubble up', from e- 'out' + bullire 'to boil'
exuberant, effervescent, buoyant
people or moods that seem to bubble over with good spirits

examples: The crowd was ebullient as the headliner walked on stage.
She gave an ebullient toast that had the whole table laughing.
vocab.ex: The crowd was ebullient as the headliner walked on stage.

spanish.meaning: Give me a shout / hit me up
spanish.note: In casual Mexican Spanish, 'echar un grito' means to get in touch, usually by call or message. People say it when making loose plans or ending a chat.

dialog.es: Voy a estar por tu zona el sábado.
dialog.en: I'll be in your area on Saturday.

dialog.es: ¡Qué bien! Échame un grito cuando llegues.
dialog.en: Great! Hit me up when you get here.
Okay, I'll hit you up.
Perfect, see you there.

spanish.use: Say it when you want a friend to get in touch about plans.

spanish.note: In Mexican Spanish, 'me late' means something sounds good or appeals to you, and it works for plans, ideas and offers. Its opposite is 'no me late', I'm not feeling it.

dialog.es: ¿Qué tal si cenamos en el mercado y luego caminamos?
dialog.en: How about dinner at the market and then a walk?

dialog.es: Me late la idea. ¿A qué hora?
dialog.en: I like that idea. What time?

dialog.es: Como a las siete, para agarrar mesa.
dialog.en: Around seven, so we can get a table.
Perfect, see you there.

spanish.use: Say it when a friend proposes a plan and you like it.

spanish.note: A very common Mexican way to say yes to a plan. Órale is an all-purpose exclamation (alright, wow, come on) and va means 'it's on'.

dialog.es: ¿Nos vemos a las siete para unos tacos?
dialog.en: Want to meet at seven for tacos?
Alright, let's do it!

dialog.es: Yo llego primero y pido mesa.
dialog.en: I'll get there first and get a table.
Perfect, see you there.

spanish.use: Say it when a friend proposes a plan and you are in.

spanish.meaning: Can you give me a hand?
spanish.note: Literally 'do you throw me the hand?'. Everyday Mexican for asking for help, from carrying boxes to fixing a problem.

cards.en: Give me a hand with this
Can I help you with something?

dialog.es: Voy a mover este sillón y está bien pesado.
dialog.en: I'm going to move this couch and it's really heavy.
Can you give me a hand?
Sure, where do I grab it?

dialog.es: Tú de ese lado, yo de este.
dialog.en: You on that side, me on this one.

spanish.use: Say it to a friend or coworker when you need help with something that takes two people.

options: Can you give me a hand?

spanish.meaning: Can you give me a ride?
spanish.note: 'Aventón' is the everyday Mexican word for a lift. You'll also hear 'raite', borrowed from English 'ride'.

dialog.es: Se me fue el camión y ya voy tarde.
dialog.en: I missed the bus and I'm already late.
I'm headed downtown.
Can you give me a ride?
Sure, hop in.

spanish.use: Say it to a friend or coworker who's driving where you're going.

options: Can you give me a ride?
Can you tell me the time?

spanish.note: Very common in Mexico for anything you like: a costume, a song, a plan. 'Padre' here means great, not father.

dialog.en: Look at my skeleton costume.
How cool!
I made it myself.
How cool, it turned out amazing!

spanish.use: Say it when someone shows you something you genuinely like.

spanish.meaning: Give it your best! / Go for it!
spanish.note: Friendly encouragement in Mexico, said before an exam, a game or a hard task. 'Echarle ganas' means to put real effort in.

dialog.en: I have my interview tomorrow.
Give it your best!
Thanks, I'm nervous.

dialog.es: Te va a ir muy bien.
dialog.en: It's going to go great.

spanish.use: Say it to a friend about to do something hard, like a race, a pitch or a first day.

phrases: Ni modo, ya será para la próxima
Ahorita vengo, voy por unos tacos

focus.title: Reach out before the birthdays

dare.title: Ask someone for their best mistake
dare.why: Pick one person a few years ahead of you in your work or a craft you love and message or catch them today with one question: what's one mistake you're glad you made? Write their answer down word for word, ask one follow-up, and don't offer advice back.
dare.worth: People rarely get asked this, and the answers are usually the best thing they know. You walk away with a real story and a closer tie to someone who's already walked the road.

swap.title: Send one specific thank-you
swap.why: Think of someone whose work made yours easier this month. Text them one sentence naming exactly what they did and what it let you do.
swap.worth: Specific thanks lands far harder than a general one, and it costs you a minute.
